“Stable” here means stable in relation to its accidental features. A body moving in place or changing in quality does not change in the same way as the body's place or quality. Fire's heat, for example, is stable when compared with the gradual heating of water.

“Subject” means the thing described as moving. “Composite” means the subject together with its motion. For Mulla Sadra, no body is wholly stable in its existence; what remains is the body through the continuous unity of its motion.
That is, the feature through which the body is potentially moving.

This applies to substantial motion and the changing nature of things. “Joined as one” means that the body, as the receiver of motion, is enough; no separate cause is needed for a feature that belongs to its nature.

The two “new forms” are different in kind: form is what changes. The two “new matters” differ only in their readiness for form. Matter in the elements is shared and remains through changes, since motion needs a subject that continues.
The result is one continuing, flowing existence. From its imagined boundaries, the mind draws out general kinds such as human, animal, and plant.

Mulla Sadra also says that the soul is the source of all our actions and perceptions because it begins through the body but survives it. The soul has different levels. The thinkers mentioned here deny that there are real powers and natures within things; Mulla Sadra does not.
This rules out inclination as the first source, since inclination is only a secondary source.

The earlier argument treated the body's changing nearness to its goal as the cause of each stage of motion. Here the two sequences are said to cause one another in different ways. The commentator on Avicenna's Pointers defended this view by treating inclination as a middle step between fixed nature and motion. Mulla Sadra's reply still applies: the changing inclination also depends on nature.

“Renewal” here means change in substance. Accidental motion is itself an effect, so it cannot cause itself. One might say that renewal is essential to a sphere's motion, and so does not need a cause, just as Mulla Sadra says of nature. But what is only an accidental feature must ultimately depend on something substantial. Accidental features, including accidental motion, depend on substances; substantial forms are the sources of their effects. Philosophers define nature as the first source of a thing's own motion and rest. If renewal were essential to accidental motion, and nature caused its existence, then nature would be a divine cause of existence, which is impossible. For these philosophers, God gives existence to the moving thing, while nature is the direct physical source of its motion.

This means the link between renewed nature and the unchanging Source. The Arabic phrase refers back to the nature just discussed. The general question of how change connects to what does not change was already explained in detail.

“In” can mean several things. “Motion in quality” may mean that quality contains motion, as ivory contains whiteness, or that a kind falls under a wider kind, as human falls under animal. The word can also describe being in a place, in time, or in a moving thing; each relation is different. The same applies to existence and essence, or to God being in the heavens and on earth.

This is correct in the following sense: at each imagined instant, the changing thing can be understood as having another kind or class within the category in which it changes. In accidental motion, the substance receives a new kind at each instant. In substantial motion, the moving thing and its motion are one, because motion in substance exists through itself. It is itself the moving substance, so no separate subject is needed. In short, motion in substance means that a different kind of substance can be drawn from the thing at each instant.
If the original blackness and every added feature were all blackness, then two like qualities would exist in one subject. It would also make an outwardly simple quality into a compound.

In that case, the original amount would not remain; adding or separating an amount destroys it. So the subject is not the amount but what carries it—matter—unless we mean a general extension that remains through the change.

Razi means that “blackness” is a wide general kind containing many shades. As a thing grows blacker, it moves from one kind of blackness to another, but all are still black. His account also reverses the direction of change: growing blacker means moving toward blackness, not away from it. If pure black is the limit farthest from white, then change moves from a different kind into the black kind, not the other way around.

All the stages are black, and flowing blackness has no actual first or final point. Any part imagined as the final part can be divided into smaller parts. Choosing one as the true endpoint would be arbitrary.

Razi's objection is specific to his own approach. There are several replies. Motion is between pure potentiality and full actuality, so the kinds within it are potential but not wholly unreal. They are potential because the motion is continuous and its limits follow one another; each limit points to the next. The motion is also actual as one whole, even though it can be divided in thought. The changing quality may be understood both as a flowing state that does not fit neatly into time, and as one continuous span that does. The momentary kinds are potential measures of change, as are the imagined parts between any two instants. These distinctions explain how one changing reality can be actual without its stages being separate actual things. They also fit the principle that existence comes before the kinds the mind draws from it.

Razi added a short period of time between successive states so that the states would not follow one another at separate instants. But then the quality would remain unchanged during each short period, and its transition to the next state would happen all at once between them. That would rule out motion, which must be gradual and continuous.

If each position lasted for a time, then the moving thing would leave one position and reach the next in an instant. The continuous place has infinitely many positions between them, so the thing would have to jump over them. It cannot do so; it must pass through them over time.

The objection assumes that motion is an added feature that exists after its subject is already complete. The reply is that motion and the flowing quality exist together as one. The difference between them is in how we describe them, not in separate things outside the mind. The quality's existence is the motion itself.
This refers to those who say that a category has both settled and flowing kinds, such as settled and flowing quality or size.

The first argument does not work because whiteness can be part of what it is to be white without being the feature that makes white different in kind from black. That does not challenge the point made here: flow is a feature the mind draws from a flowing reality.
The change may also be described as movement from one individual of a kind or class to another.

“Beginning” may mean a state different from the thing that follows it, like a point to a line, rest to motion, or an instant to time. It may also mean the first part of a thing. Continuous things, whether settled or flowing, have no actual first part in this second sense. Here, “beginning,” “end,” “from,” and “toward” mean the first and last limits of what changes—for example, warmth and the strongest heat in a change of quality. They do not mean the periods of rest before and after motion. The motion's limits follow from its definition. A limit can be both a “from” and a “toward,” depending on the direction considered, especially in the endless motion of the celestial spheres. Each imagined part can in turn be divided without end.

The positions may be alike in kind and nature, but “the same” here means one and the same individual. A position that has ceased to exist does not return as that exact same individual. Otherwise, the same reasoning would apply to every position between the two daily positions, which would mean an endless number of positions repeating in the sphere's motion. Common sense rules this out.
“Point” is used loosely. Each position at an instant is simple, like a flowing point.
On this view, each category is related to motion in its own way. It resembles the view that knowledge belongs to the category of the thing known.

Another view says that motion belongs to the categories of acting and being acted on: motion as being moved belongs to one, and motion as moving something belongs to the other. Mulla Sadra instead sees motion as a way of existing, and the whole natural world as flowing. What he says here does not conflict with that view: being moved and moving are not motion itself, just as heating and being heated are not heat.

The highest categories do not change according to how we look at them. So it is unclear how motion could count as being acted on when viewed from the receiver, and as acting when viewed from the agent. Nor does motion become place, position, quality, size, or substance simply by being considered on its own. The point may instead be that motion in one of these five categories gives the agent and receiver the relative features of acting and being acted on.

The argument is that motion in a category requires the subject to have a different individual of that category at each instant. So the categories of acting and being acted on would need momentary individuals that exist only potentially. Motion is the subject's passage from one such individual to another. But acting and being acted on are themselves gradual states. If motion occurred within them, the subject would be moving further into a state it had not yet reached, rather than leaving one settled state for another. Leaving one gradual state for another would itself have to be gradual, which would start another motion and lead to an endless chain. The same problem arises if these categories are identified with motion itself: they are not separate, momentary individuals, but a continuing process. The deeper point is that if substantial motion occurs, the body's accidental features also move with it, since they are levels or appearances of the body's existence. Mulla Sadra recognized this result and argued for it elsewhere, though he did not fully work through all its consequences here. On this view, a body has a motion in its own substance and, through it, a motion in its place, position, size, and quality. These motions may be nested: the body's place can change because its substance changes, and it may also move from one place to another. The same applies to the other categories.

Each gradual state has infinitely many parts. If motion occurred within such a state, the subject could not leave it in a single instant. It would have to remain in each part for some time, which would make it at rest.

There is a further problem. If motion occurred in acting, then the subject would have to move from one kind of heating to another. But it cannot leave one kind of heating while still heating, or stop heating all at once and begin cooling in the next instant. Both results conflict with what motion means.

This depends on how rest is defined. If rest means that a thing stays in one place, it is the opposite of motion. If it means the absence of motion in something that can move, it is the absence of a capacity, not the opposite. Avicenna discusses this in The Healing.

The philosophers say that the outermost sphere has a position relative to the other bodies, even though it has no place around it. Mulla Sadra says that it does have a place, since place is a kind of dimension.

A moving thing moves toward a goal that completes it. Each stage of motion is a first completion compared with the stage before it, but only potential compared with the stage after it. Motion therefore has degrees of completion. This also shows that a thing cannot move naturally from greater strength to lesser strength: motion is a gradual passage from potentiality to actuality. When something seems to weaken, such as a bitter liquid gradually cooling, another feature may be replacing its heat. The body's changing features are part of its changing existence, so this need not be strange.
This makes clear that Mulla Sadra does not regard any kind of motion as lacking degrees. It also rules out motion from one equal stage to another, where no stage is more or less complete.

The earlier discussion showed that blackness itself cannot be the subject of change. Here the point is how change in quality works. A flowing blackness has a weak unity when compared with settled blackness: it lies between pure potentiality and complete actuality. Taken without that comparison, it has a broad unity that includes all the shades of black. It resembles the continuous motion considered between its limits.
This explanation keeps us from treating the lasting blackness and the added degrees as two separate things outside the mind. The distinction is made by the mind.

In a change of quality, there can be something like a lasting base and added features, but the distinction between them exists only in thought. The difference here is that those particular features pass away while the base remains. In the present account, the apparent branches pass away within the lasting base.

If what a thing is were the basic reality, then all the different kinds would exist separately in actuality, and the changes between them would contain infinitely many actual divisions. But if existence is primary, it is like a thread that holds them together; the different kinds are distinctions the mind draws from it. Even the view held by Aristotle’s followers that existence is primary but made up of entirely distinct simple realities would still support the argument, since the multiplicity would be in actual existence. Here, however, there is one continuous, flowing existence. Mulla Sadra does not accept that other view, which is why he interprets its wording in another way.

A person’s own existence has stages corresponding to the seven inner dimensions of human life. Notice these stages in yourselves, then turn toward the simple reality that encompasses all existence. The three results drawn here are, first, that existence is what is real; second, that a thing can change in its very being; and third, that many things are united in one reality. The author’s expression of wonder is fitting: if the unity of a changing quality is astonishing, how much more astonishing is the soul, the great sign of God and one of His greatest wonders! Lord, deepen my wonder at You.

This raises two problems: how can one thing belong to many kinds, and how can one thing be bodily in its origin but later exist without a body, as Mulla Sadra says of the soul? There is also the problem of what remains the subject through change. The following discussion addresses these points.

In The Divine Witnesses, Mulla Sadra says that change and nonpersistence belong to existence, while permanence belongs to what a thing is. The two claims can be reconciled by noticing that the present discussion treats different stages as forms of one continuous individual existence. The mind draws different kinds from those stages. In the other work, he looks at differences in existence and at the shared meanings in our concepts. General words can apply to very different realities: “animal,” for example, can refer to a bodily animal, an imaginal being, or a spiritual one; “rational” can mean capable of reason or actually reasoning, as with an intellect that has become actual or the Active Intellect.

The earlier reply—that motion itself is one continuous individual, with its different kinds existing only potentially—would already explain the unity of motion without requiring a stable subject. A stable subject alone cannot make separate, unrelated features one motion. A subject must remain in accidental motion because accidents exist in a subject and take their identity from it. Substance exists in itself, so it needs no further subject to remain one. In substantial motion, the material substance is both the moving thing and the motion: its own existence is renewed. A thing made of heat, if heat were a substance, would be both hot and heating. A fixed subject is needed only for accidental motion. But since accidental features also change with the motion of substance, the unity of the substance supports the unity of those motions too.

One might ask how matter can become individual before it is individual, or exist before it exists. The true cause of matter and its individual identity is a single separate being. The general form—some form or other—works together with it as a lesser cause. That is enough for matter, which is pure potentiality. A general cause can also account for what is absent, since absence is a light burden for a cause. “Some form” may also mean an eternal, all-embracing form, whose generality means that it contains all particular forms. It relates to particular forms as continuous motion relates to the separate positions we imagine within it, or as a flowing instant relates to the parts of time. The author means a real bodily kind, not a mere idea or a general kind that disappears into different defining features.

In the usual account of coming to be and passing away, each form takes matter's place after the prior form has ended. On the view of substantial motion, the forms follow one another as parts of one continuous existence. This continuous form keeps matter actual. The different forms are boundaries the mind draws within it, just as different places are boundaries within motion from place to place. The full account will come in the discussion of matter and form.

The phrase “so this should be possible too” is a parenthetical point. “Body” here means a particular kind of body that acts as matter, not the general kind that can be said of different kinds of body. A general kind cannot make matter actual or give it one continuing identity.
This is even more likely for particular forms, since they are more fully defined than bodily form, and matter formed as a body is closer to being one and lasting.

Nature exists through particular examples, so we can prove substantial motion by saying that the formed matter remains while the changing specific form flows through it. Not every substance flows: intellects, and souls considered in themselves, are not material and do not change in their own nature.

An amount cannot remain unchanged when another amount is added to it or separated from it. That is why philosophers say that quantity can be divided in thought, but not broken apart into separate quantities. Prime matter can be broken apart because it is not itself a fixed amount and can receive separation or connection. If we say that the two amounts after division are the same as the first, this refers to the subject that remains, not to the quantities themselves, which are simple outside the mind.

According to these philosophers, animal powers are not separate from the body; they are present in the subtle bodily spirit. Nothing in this account remains unchanged. Change is even more obvious in plants, which have no sensation or voluntary motion—powers that point toward a level beyond matter.

If we consider the plant through its motion, the stages are potential; if we ask what stays as its original basis, they are actual, as Avicenna says. No one part of its duration is more important than another. A continuous existence is one personal identity, just as a length remains one even though it can be divided without end in thought.

Avicenna first says that one form needs one matter, so how could it take on many matters through nourishment? He then suggests that the near matter may be many while the first matter is one. He rejects this too: if a form exists throughout the matter it shapes, how could one form be one while its immediate subjects are many? “Form” here means the specific form.

The earlier and later powers are alike in that both exist throughout their subjects. Neither is a separate feature laid over the subject, as relations can be. Neither power exists apart from the subject, even in an imaginal form. So when the later power disappears, the earlier one disappears too.

The connection between the parts is only by relation. If it were a true continuous connection, the parts would not be separate individuals. Avicenna does not refute this option here because the earlier points already show why it fails: it would make the instants follow one another with no duration between them.
“Flows from” means that the later form comes from God through the original source.

Animals have some original parts formed from the bodies of their parents, such as bones, nerves, and ligaments. Other parts, such as flesh and fat, are formed from blood. If the original parts disappear, the other parts also disappear, but not the other way around. It is not clear whether this applies to plants and to some animals.

This refers to the “lords of the species,” the separate patterns for kinds of things proposed by the Illuminationist school. In The Journey of the Soul, Mulla Sadra says this is the right view, though Avicenna mentions it without settling the question.

This is an exception to the claim that plants cannot have original and secondary parts. Parts that look alike may differ in reality: some may be foundational, others added later. The same distinction is clear in animals.

“First matter” here means matter considered in the upward development of things. It cannot be the stable subject because it has weak existence and unity, and the different forms that arise in it divide it. But matter has two kinds of unity. One comes from the form and disappears when a single connected form is divided. The other belongs to matter itself and remains whether the forms are connected or come in succession. Separation does not destroy this second unity. Mulla Sadra later says that prime matter is the subject of expansion and contraction; he has already said that it is the subject of nature's flow.

This follows from the argument about division and connection that establishes matter. The specific forms stand above bodily form not only in the order of definitions but also in the order of existence: bodily form exists, and specific form exists at a higher level. No bodily form exists without some specific form, whether celestial, elemental, simple, or compound.
Another reply: the claim that one amount destroys another applies to settled amounts, not to amounts that are parts of a gradual motion.

Compared with real existence, all these general kinds and defining features are necessary features of a thing. They count as parts only when the mind considers what the thing is. They can change without destroying the thing if its final defining feature remains, since that feature gathers the earlier forms and their completions. For Mulla Sadra, the true defining feature is real existence, which gives a thing its unity and simplicity.

Matter's persistence is easier to see in expansion and contraction because it remains through the change and is not tied to one particular amount. The body is harder to see as the subject because changing amounts reveal that the measured body also changes. Its general kind remains only as a universal nature or an eternal reality, which is hard for the imagination and the limited intellect to accept. The distinction between original and later parts in plants and animals may also show why matter can be the subject in both kinds of motion.

The final defining feature of a complete human being is actual reason, or the Active Intellect. The old definition of a human as a “mortal rational animal” uses “mortal” in the sense of voluntary death. In a complete human being, this final feature gathers all the changing and passing forms: the defining features of lower kinds become general kinds in relation to it, and their forms become like its matter. It is the form of forms and the feature that gathers what is scattered.

The stages on the way to the final human form are changes that bring greater completion, not forms that are simply put on and taken off. There is no loss followed by gain, but gain followed by gain, and finding followed by finding, without end.

Another reason a subject remains through substantial motion is that bodily natures are delicate traces of higher realities. Their stable aspect comes from their connection to the separate patterns of their kinds.

These intellectual forms do not exist separately for themselves; they are relations to the rational soul. One might ask how an intellectual idea can be an image if, as Mulla Sadra says, knowing a general kind means seeing its separate pattern. An image seen from far away can represent what we later see at close range after returning often to the world of intellect. “Image” is a broad term: it includes things sensed outwardly or inwardly, and things understood by the intellect.

This gives another account of what remains through motion. Some features mentioned above belong to the agent, some to the receiver, some to what is received, and some to the category in which change occurs. Each helps preserve the body's unity. If natural form itself is flowing, it may seem unable to provide that unity. The reply is that form has a continuous individual through time, both as the middle stage of motion and as the whole connected process. Matter, then, has what gives it multiplicity and what gives it unity. Its unity does not come only from one separate being; it is supported by these other relations too.

The four accidental motions are like a body whose soul is substantial motion, the renewal of nature. Time is like a body whose soul is timeless order. Timeless order is in turn like a body whose soul is eternity. The containers relate to one another as their contents do. What is eternal surrounds what is timeless, and both surround what belongs to time. Timeless order, in all its parts, relates to time as a day relates to its hours, minutes, and seconds—or as the flowing instant relates to time. The point is that changing motions and times are stable in relation to separate beings and to the source of both separate and bodily beings.

Nature that comes from the soul is a lower level of the soul and exists through it as its effect. The other nature belongs to the elements and exists within them. The first is naturally ready to obey the soul; the second is made to obey. Fatigue comes from the second, not the first. Physicians and natural philosophers use “nature” for the power that manages the body, preserves its health, and pushes illness away. Plato uses it for the divine power that acts in the body by God's permission—the first kind.

This alludes to the Qur'anic account in which God tells heaven and earth to come willingly or unwillingly, and they answer that they come willingly. This applies to nature that comes from the soul, which obeys willingly, and the nature of the elements, which obeys under compulsion. The speech is by God through the soul, which is a divine mystery and a command from the Lord. As Rumi says, every voice comes from the King, even when it comes through a servant's throat. God spoke this way to the heavens and earth of the visible world. His word is complete and the Pen has dried in relation to God's eternal reality, though the world remains in a state of renewal for beings confined by place and time. The earth and its like answer willingly when they see their own beauty as a display of God's names and qualities. Their journey toward God is a source of great joy. If they did not make that journey, they would remain in the pit of matter and the unjust town of ignorance, and suffer a deep loss. At first they resist being moved from their familiar places because they do not understand. Ignorance is the root of evil; knowledge is the root of good.

A clearer distinction would be between two types of helpers: those that belong to the soul and obey it by their nature, such as senses that follow it into the imaginal world and the afterlife; and those that belong to the body and obey it only indirectly. Mulla Sadra identifies the two kinds here with the sources of motion in quality and quantity, and with those in place and position. One might object that both are the same nature that was just discussed. The distinction may be that “nature” earlier means the body's elements, while the powers here come from the soul; or that the earlier term means the lasting root shared by bodily and plant-like powers, while these are its separate levels and branches. This resembles the debate over whether the animal soul is the sum of all its powers or the ruling power of estimation. The better view is that the animal soul is the shared root of those powers, existing in each at its own level.

“Willingly” and “under force” describe how the imagination and thought experience these powers. In themselves, both kinds are natural: both the powers that attract and push, and the powers that move the body. Even walking depends on a nature that is ready to obey the soul, and this nature remains with the soul in the afterlife. Mulla Sadra's contrast is between what is naturally ready to obey and what is made to obey.

These powers serve the intellect only when their actions are directed toward rational ends. Otherwise, the outward and inward powers of perception belong to the animal soul, like the powers that move the body. The note's qualification matters because imagination and estimation do not, by themselves, submit to reason.

This obedient nature belongs to the imaginal body, just as the power spread through the muscles belongs to the physical body. The powers that come from the soul are its domain and the place where its light appears. This answers those who deny bodily resurrection and accept only spiritual survival. They argue that particular bodily perceptions need particular bodily organs, which disappear when the body falls apart. But the soul has its own sight, hearing, and other senses, as well as a body in the afterlife.

My first objection is that this leaves natural powers unable to act, which is as unacceptable as denying them altogether. Some theologians who reject natural causes avoid the problem by saying that powers act only on things outside their own subjects, or that existence flows through nature. Second, why should a spatial relation be required to connect cause and effect? What relation could be closer than the union between a power and its subject? Sadra and many other philosophers say that an agent acts through its very being. In The Journey of the Soul, Sadra compares spatial relation in bodily action with the spiritual nearness through which immaterial beings receive the flow of existence. In Origin and Return, he says that a cause and what it affects do not always need to be separate, as when form acts on matter. So why require position when a power acts on something outside its own matter? For action within its own matter, the author may be applying the rule “consider the outcomes, not the starting points.” Third, even if we accept the argument, it may show only that action is bodily because the matter that receives the power has a position. This is all the proof establishes: if a thing exists through matter, its action depends on matter, and matter exists positionally. This argument also appears in The Divine Witnesses. It fits the Illuminationist view that separate forms for kinds—horizontal intellects—produce all the effects in our world.

This argument works only if there is a gradual change that necessarily belongs to a natural kind and is directly intended by its nature, rather than occurring as a side effect. The commentator denies both claims about natural kinds and says the fuller discussion belongs elsewhere.

If motion were not an effect of nature, it would not come after nature; it would exist together with it, in the same primary mode of existence, rather than as a secondary feature that follows from it.

Calling form and matter “co-causes” means that form is not a cause in the usual sense. Existence flows first through form and then through matter. There is no shared causal action between them: a bodily cause acts only through position, and form and matter are united rather than positioned apart from each other. Still, causation does not always require separation. Sadra says in Origin and Return that form causes matter, and philosophers also say that a defining feature causes the general kind, though they are united in what the statement describes.

The examples show that we name the subject by a feature that follows from it. Strictly speaking, a logical defining feature is a feature of the thing: a general idea given in answer to the question “What is it, in its substance?”

There is a subtle point here. Taken as features that belong to the individual, these accidents are signs of individuality, since an individuating feature must apply to the individual. In that respect they are one with their subject, though they are a second level of its existence and an outward appearance of it. We must preserve both levels without losing the unity of the subject. These necessary features are not like unity or individuality, which do not follow existence as later features; they are more like mathematical body and natural body, which, in the experts' view, differ only in how they are considered. This is the way to understand the argument without erasing the nine categories of accidents.

Matter, attachment to matter, the possibility of becoming something else, and motion are what make a thing distinct from the higher reality. Where the marks of possibility, especially readiness to become something else, prevail, a thing exists because God brings it into being and continues because God sustains it. But where these marks disappear, so that nothing remains to be attained and even the thing’s possibility is hidden in the light of eternity, it exists through God’s own existence and lasts through His lasting existence. Some of the author’s contemporaries missed this distinction and criticised him in their writings. I have discussed it in my notes on the section concerning divine things in this book; anyone who wishes can consult them.

Worship joined with reflection, free from seeing anything besides the One worshipped, leads to complete servanthood. And servanthood is, in its very essence, lordship. It is as though you are being told to become pure intellect, so that you may know the intellect that endures through God’s enduring existence—not through a separate act of preservation or through its own independent being. It has no existence of its own, just as the meaning of a connecting word does not stand alone. Or “those who worship” may refer to the powers and natures whose very substance is constantly renewed; their worship is expressed in their being. This message then announces their arrival at their goals.
“Then another form must take its place” and the preceding argument are also refuted by motion in quality and other kinds of motion.
This refers to the argument that instants would have to follow one another.
Matter is also brought into being as an individual.
Here, “form” means the form that underlies a thing's actual motion, like the middle stage of motion, not the general idea of form.
This answers the claim that the kind either remains through change or not.

“Opposite” may mean any opposite, including intermediate opposites, or it may mean only a strict opposite. Avicenna's argument is also refuted by kinds of motion, such as motion in amount, that do not involve opposites.

Avicenna's view is clear: time measures motion, and a measure follows what it measures in either flowing or remaining fixed. The majority view is that a motion considered as one whole from beginning to end is stable and has no parts that pass away; only the path of motion has parts, and they exist only in imagination. If motion itself cannot have parts that pass away, time alone must be inherently unstable. The commentator says their further account of how time's measure remains is another matter. A more precise explanation is that division depends on first treating something as a measure. Without a measure, there is no whole or part, small or large. Philosophers treat division as an essential feature of quantity; division in a physical body is only secondary. On this view, time's parts pass away in themselves, while motion's parts do so only by extension.

Motion means the renewal of a thing; but renewal, considered by itself, is not a separate thing. This resembles the claim that a thing's existence is its being real: that reality cannot itself be another thing, or it would need yet another reality to make it real. Motion, then, is like a grammatical particle that makes sense only in relation to a noun. It is not a separate moving thing or a separate measure. The claim that motion and time are themselves unstable therefore misses the point: they are the renewal of something, its measure, and the thing renewed.

Philosophers and theologians agree that coming into being is not the same as the thing that comes into being, or the process through which it comes to be. Philosophers say coming into being exists in the mind, with only its source in the thing itself. The theologian Abu Hashim says it is a state that is neither existent nor nonexistent: it is not nonexistent because a real thing can be described as coming into being, but it cannot itself be a separate existent, since then it would either be eternal or need to come into being in turn, leading to an endless chain.
A possible thing has both a nature and existence: existence drives nonexistence away, and “existent” describes the relation between the thing's nature and its existence.

The verse may refer to mountains changing as one form after another comes to be through substantial motion. Or it may point to the human being's gradual ascent toward fuller existence: through motion in place and in substance, life develops through plant and animal stages toward the fully actual human being. This ascent continues through successive cycles because God's outpouring of existence never ends.

This refers to repeated renewal and to the gradual ascent through stages, from human society and plant life toward actual humanity. On the view that the Day of Resurrection includes all the timeless and temporal days, the transformation of the physical earth into an imaginal and afterlife earth takes place in the intermediate world. Reason and scripture agree that this is the first resurrection, though reason calls the earlier stages resurrection too. The heavens undergo similar transformations. These stages do not destroy the identity of what changes, because the process is continuous and its lasting basis is the face of God. Individual identity comes from existence.

God wills and brings about this change because the Necessary Being is necessary in every respect. God's will is necessary, not a possibility that might or might not be fulfilled. What is possible for creatures occurs within God's will under necessity.

The wording is inverted: the point is that a thing whose causes of preservation are also its causes of destruction must have an existence interwoven with passing away—that is, an existence in motion. Coming into being includes passing away at every stage. Another reading gives no proof of substantial motion: the same powers that preserve a thing can also destroy it. Sight may find something desirable, and desire may consume it. Bodily powers can also bring about illness through excess or restraint. Natural philosophers likewise said that the body's innate heat is both a cause of life and a cause of death.

Souls, as rays of the intellects, are what give bodies their stability and light. Bodies themselves are dark and unstable because of their distance in space, separation in time, and dependence on matter. Their lasting and luminous aspect comes from the holy intellects. The commentator adds a short verse: “The mill wheel turns the water over and over; the moon's reflection and the stars remain.”
